The paper surveys robotic foundation models (RFMs) as large‑scale, multimodal systems intended to serve as a “generalist core” for collaborative cobots in high‑mix, low‑volume industrial settings. It contrasts these models with narrow, single‑purpose approaches and argues that, while modern cobot hardware meets safety and payload constraints (0.5–20 kg, low power), the principal barrier to deployment is the lack of robust, adaptable models that can be reused across tasks, sensor configurations, and multimodal commands without extensive engineering.

To quantify this gap, the authors construct three reproducible literature corpora: a primary set of 1 025 highly relevant RFM papers, an industrial‑implication set of 125 manually vetted works, and 113 auxiliary sources. The corpora are assembled via an automated Python pipeline that combines ASQS queries, duplicate removal, LLM‑based relevance filtering, and manual enrichment. From these sources they derive eleven inter‑dependent industrial implications—adaptability, safety certification, human‑centric interaction, robustness, precision, real‑time edge inference, cost‑effectiveness, explainability, multimodal perception, standardized benchmarking, and data‑efficient learning—mapped to 47 concrete deployment attributes, forming a 149‑item criteria catalogue (517 implication‑attribute cells).

Applying the catalogue through an automated GPT‑5.1 pipeline to 324 manipulation‑capable RFMs yields 48 276 binary decisions. Overall maturity scores are uniformly low: the highest‑rated model (Gemini Robotics 1.5) attains an overall score of 0.12 and a peak I1 (adaptability) score of 0.44, meaning it satisfies roughly one‑tenth of the criteria. Across the corpus, research concentrates on adaptability/flexibility (I1), benchmarking (I10), and data usage (I11), while safety/compliance (I2), human‑robot interaction (I3), real‑time robustness (I6), and cost‑effectiveness/integration (I7) are markedly under‑represented. Roughly half of the models meet I1, ≤5 % address safety, redundancy, or cost, ≤20 % show explainability, and 45–49 % satisfy repeatability or flexible data‑type acceptance. No model scores non‑zero on all eleven criteria, and total scores range from 0.01 to 0.12, far below the authors’ 0.5 threshold for comprehensive industrial readiness.

The authors interpret these findings as evidence that current RFMs remain laboratory‑oriented, advancing isolated dimensions without delivering the safety‑critical, low‑latency, cost‑effective capabilities required for real‑world factory deployment. They call for layered architectures separating planning, verification, and safety; for evaluation protocols that capture edge‑level latency, dynamic sensor/tool changes, distribution shifts, failure recovery, and long‑horizon operation; and for benchmarks that report energy, latency, and safety metrics across heterogeneous hardware.

Supplementary material includes: Appendix A, a bibliography of 55 recent surveys (2023‑2025) on vision‑language‑action and multimodal foundations; Appendix B, the raw systematic query strings used to assemble the corpora (tables could not be reliably reconstructed); Appendix C, the detailed industrial‑implication rubric defining the eight primary categories and associated benchmark themes; and Appendix D, the automatically generated RFM overview showing proportional applicability scores per implication dimension, with explicit caveats that these scores lack empirical validation and confidence intervals. The work thus maps industrial demands to a detailed criteria set, demonstrates that existing RFMs fall far short, and outlines a research agenda focused on safety, real‑time performance, integration, and comprehensive benchmarking to bridge the gap to reliable industrial autonomy.
